title: Re'eh: as you were blessed (Deuteronomy 16:17)
hookLine: each gives according to the blessing they have received

lines: THE VERSE SAYS IT OUT LOUD.
cards: Someone at the office is leaving, and an envelope goes around for a gift. Somebody suggests everyone put in twenty dollars. And immediately it's awkward.
For the manager, twenty is nothing. For the part-time assistant saving for rent, it's a real bite. A flat amount sounds fair, and isn't.
A percentage sounds cold, and is fairer. Nobody quite knows how to say it out loud. The last verse of Re'eh says it, in a handful of words, about pilgrims arriving at the Temple three times a year.

teach.b: Three times a year, the chapter says, at Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, every man of Israel is to appear at the place God chooses. And, in the old Jewish translation: "they shall not appear before the LORD empty."
Every pilgrim brings something. But how much? The same sentence answers: "every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD thy God which He hath given thee."

teach.h: K'MATNAT YADO: THE GIFT OF HIS HAND.
teach.b: In Hebrew, ish k'matnat yado: each person according to the gift of his hand. No flat fee. The measure is what you've been given.
The Mishnah, in tractate Chagigah, works it out for the festival offerings.
Someone with many mouths to feed and little money brings what they can, shaped to their household. Someone with much brings more. Same command, different amounts.

teach.h: A GIVER, NOT JUST A RECEIVER.
teach.b: Nobody comes empty: even the poorest pilgrim brings something, and so stands in the courtyard as a giver, not just a receiver. And nobody hides behind a small number when they've been given a great deal.
The verse shames no one. It asks one quiet question: what have you been blessed with?

This verse also ends a Torah reading used on the last days of the festivals, and in many synagogues those are days when the memorial prayer, Yizkor, is said, and people pledge gifts in memory of those they've lost.
Giving according to what you were given, including the people who gave it.

how: The reading that ends with this verse is used on the last days of the pilgrimage festivals, and in many synagogues, when Yizkor is recited on those days, people pledge charity in memory of relatives who have died.

games.q: a pilgrim with little money and a big family arrives at the festival. what does the verse ask?
o: bring the same as the wealthiest.
bring something, according to what they have.
games.why: not empty, and according to the blessing. the measure is what you've been given.

practice: Take honest stock, and not just of money: time, health, a skill, free evenings, patience with kids. Which of these do you have more of this season than the people around you?
Picture one place that surplus could go, in proportion: if you have little money but a lot of time, the gift might be time.

carryVoice: Your line: according to your blessing. Nobody comes empty, and nobody is measured by someone else's gift. That's day five hundred one.
